To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“The distribution of extracellular water is shifted to the plasma during the post‐hemorrhage transcapillary refueling phase.”
the ratio of plasma volume (PV) to interstitial fluid (ISF) volume (ISF) is increased after blood loss and that this increase is not due to a decrease in PV or an increase in ISF.
The distribution of extracellular fluids is biased toward the vascular space during posthemorrhagic transvascular refilling.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a study of the distribution of the extracellular fluid after hemorrhage and the restoration of blood volume.
the dynamic redistribution of extracellular fluid after hemorrhagic shock.
the dynamic distribution of the extracellular space after blood loss.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the dynamic distribution of salt and water after blood loss in man is a complex process that involves a number of interrelated factors and that the final result is dependent on the amount of blood loss.
the distribution of extraceullular fluid after hemorrhage is biased in favor of the plasma, but not as much as the ratio of plasma volume: interstitial fluid volume would imply.
the dynamic distribution of balanced salt and mannitol infusion after blood loss in man, during post‐hemorrhage transcapillary refiling, is biased toward the blood plasma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the interstitial fluid volume is increased by 10 to 20% after hemorrhage and that the plasma volume is increased by an equivalent amount.
the interstitial space is not refilled after hemorrhage.

, in the absence of an osmotic gradient across capillary walls, the distribution of fluid is biased toward plasma, but in the presence of a large osmotic gradient, the distribution is biased toward interstitial fluid.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the distribution of salt and mannitol is biased towards the plasma, and this bias is not eliminated by the infusion of salt and manniltol solutions, even when these solutions are administered at the same rate as the blood loss.
the distribution of salt and mannitol infusions is biased in favor of plasma volume during transcapillary refiling.
the distribution of salt and mannitol is dynamic and is influenced by the state of the vascular bed.
